tagline: Along the St. Johns, a river road beneath moss-draped trees
intro: State Road 13 winds along the St. Johns River through pine and palmetto barrens, oak hammocks and swamps beneath moss-draped trees. The William Bartram Scenic and Historic Highway received Florida Scenic Highway designation on October 31, 2005. The state program emphasizes the corridor’s natural landscape, parks and cultural destinations, with wide trails running beside the road. The canoe trail bearing Bartram’s name follows a different course, from Durbin Creek to Julington Creek.

The legislature had named SR 13 the William Bartram Scenic Highway in 1980. Residents concerned about development later sought designation through the Florida Scenic Highways Program. Working with St. Johns County, the corridor group completed the eligibility process in 2002; a management plan followed in 2005. The group recommended standards for public spaces, architecture and tree protection. The road’s namesake traveled here by water: in 1774, naturalist William Bartram bought a small sailboat at Cow Ford, the future site of Jacksonville, before continuing to Switzerland and Fort Picolata.

Begin at Julington Creek Bridge and follow the river’s east bank south through Switzerland. Bartram landed at Francis Philip Fatio’s plantation there during his 1774 river journey. The road runs south from Julington Creek Bridge for about 17 miles, ending at Ward’s Creek.
notice: Moss-draped trees line a corridor of pine and palmetto barrens, oak hammocks and swamps.

moments.title: Julington Creek
moments.text: Julington Creek widens into the St. Johns River at the southern edge of Jacksonville. SR 13 crosses the creek on a bridge; a ferry once crossed these waters. Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote of visits to the creek in Palmetto Leaves, published in 1873 while she was living in Mandarin. Upstream, Durbin Creek joins Julington Creek; the peninsula between them forms part of Julington-Durbin Creek Preserve. The Bartram Canoe Trail connects the two creeks, while Julington Creek flows toward Old Bull Bay at the border of Duval and St. Johns counties.

moments.title: Switzerland
moments.text: Switzerland’s name comes from Francis Philip Fatio’s New Switzerland plantation on the east bank of the St. Johns. Fatio moved there in 1774 and named the plantation for his birthplace. That year, William Bartram arrived by sailboat during his travels through Florida. Under Spanish rule, the plantation became Nueva Suiza and produced maize, citrus fruit and cotton for sale. Its workforce included 86 enslaved people and four free Black people. Merchant ships carried plantation products, including timber, away from its river landing; troops, supplies and messages also passed through on their way between St. Augustine and Spanish outposts.

moments.title: Fort Picolata
moments.text: Fort Picolata and Fort San Francisco de Pupo controlled a ferry crossing where the St. Johns River narrows. The crossing lay on the old trail to the Spanish province of Apalachee. After destruction during the War of Jenkins’ Ear, Picolata was rebuilt in 1755 as a coquina stone tower, two and a half stories high. In a 1774 report to his patron, Dr. John Fothergill, William Bartram described the fort as newly repaired. His later Travels instead described it as dismantled and deserted. Coquina for the rebuilt fort was brought to this crossing of El Camino Real, the Royal Road into the interior.
